title: One Giant Clam Contains a Month‑by‑Month Diary of the Great Barrier Reef’s Climate 200 Years Ago - Nautilus
gist: Researchers including Sean Ulm read the growth record in a single giant clam (Tridacna gigas) shell to reconstruct month-by-month climate conditions around 200 years ago at Jiigurru (Lizard Island Group) in the northern Great Barrier Reef. The article excerpt is a short teaser describing the method's premise.

themes.theme: Giant clam shells as climate archives

insights.claim: Tridacna gigas, the world's largest living bivalve, can reach 1.2 metres, weigh more than 200 kilograms and live for over a century.
insights.speaker: Sean Ulm
insights.so_what: Century-plus lifespans make individual clams long-duration natural sensors, extending reef climate records back before instrumental data.
insights.locator: As the world’s largest living bivalve

insights.claim: Giant clams record their daily life in their shell growth over their long lives, effectively creating an 'autobiographical shell diary' that researchers can read.
insights.speaker: Sean Ulm
insights.so_what: Sub-annual resolution proxies allow seasonal-scale reconstructions of past ocean conditions, useful baselines for assessing current reef stress.
insights.quote: these clams record their daily life in their shells, creating an autobiographical shell diary
insights.locator: As the world’s largest living bivalve

themes.theme: Historical climate reconstruction at Lizard Island

insights.claim: New research used a single giant clam shell diary to reconstruct month-by-month climate conditions at Jiigurru (the Lizard Island Group) in the northern Great Barrier Reef, roughly 200 years ago.
insights.speaker: Sean Ulm
insights.so_what: Pre-industrial monthly baselines for the Great Barrier Reef sharpen comparisons of today's warming and bleaching risk against natural variability.
insights.quote: we read one of these shell diaries to reconstruct month-by-month climate conditions at Jiigurru
